extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, science journalists, and readers interested in scientific publishing and misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices for detecting, preventing, and responding to inappropriate image manipulation in scientific publications, aimed at journals, institutions, and researchers. Covers pre- and post-publication screening, tool validation, investigations, and corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where ethical lines are drawn between acceptable and unacceptable image adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: “To avoid such a situation, it is important to understand where the ethical lines are drawn between acceptable and unacceptable image adjustment.” (Rossner & Yamada quoted.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish routine, non-deceptive image adjustments (e.g., brightness/contrast for clarity applied to the whole image) from manipulations that alter the scientific meaning (e.g., splicing, selective retouching, duplicating features). Educate authors and reviewers on those boundaries to prevent accusations of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication image screening by journals using digital image experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can and have used “digital image experts” to screen submitted manuscripts for problematic image manipulations before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a pre-publication screening program staffed by trained image integrity screeners (examples: Journal of Cell Biology). Many journals adopted screening early on; journals should (re)adopt or maintain such screening rather than leaving detection to after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take post-publication community critiques (e.g., PubPeer) seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms like PubPeer and independent sleuths have become a major force in flagging image and other integrity problems; publishers, journals, and institutions can’t ignore these critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish processes to monitor, assess, and respond to community-raised concerns promptly. Treat well-reasoned public critiques as actionable leads rather than dismissing them because they originate outside formal channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation requirement for automated/AI image-detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and publishers are developing automated and AI tools to detect image manipulation, but validation of these instruments so far is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before wide deployment, validate detection tools for sensitivity, specificity, false-positive rates, and reproducibility. Encourage transparency about algorithm performance and independent evaluation to ensure tools 'work' at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate beautification from falsification; assess intent and severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all image adjustments are equal: some may be “beautification” while others show signs of intentional and inappropriate manipulation that could indicate fabrication or falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations and corrective actions should consider whether adjustments were cosmetic or deceptive, and whether there was intent to mislead. Severity and intent should inform whether a correction, retraction, or misconduct finding is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish prompt, accurate corrections and retractions when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must correct or retract articles that contain manipulated images; failure to publish promised corrections (as described in the Science example) undermines trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have clear, timely workflows for issuing corrections or retractions. Publicly document corrections and ensure they are implemented correctly in the literature to maintain integrity and public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should avoid delay and secrecy in investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions sometimes ignore allegations until they cannot, then conduct secretive investigations while distancing prominent figures from the work — a criticized 'playbook.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct timely, transparent investigations with clear timelines and communication; avoid unnecessary obfuscation or tactics that appear designed to wait out public attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage use of third-party pre-publication screening services
rubrics_metrics.description: Private companies (e.g., Proofig) offer image-screening services to authors, journals, and publishers to minimize the risk of costly investigations and retractions after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and journals can consider third-party screening as a risk-reduction step; evaluate vendors for accuracy and reliability and incorporate screening into submission or editorial workflows where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to and support whistleblowers and independent sleuths
rubrics_metrics.description: Whistleblowers and voluntary sleuths (e.g., Elisabeth Bik and others) have played a crucial role in identifying problematic images and other issues in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create channels that protect and facilitate reporting, ensure allegations are examined by qualified experts, and avoid retaliatory or dismissive responses to legitimate concerns raised from outside official channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental expectation: do not manipulate images to mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlying all other measures, researchers should refrain from manipulating images in ways that change scientific meaning; 'not manipulate images in the first place' is the central message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote ethical training, clear author guidelines on acceptable image processing, and foster a research culture that prizes integrity over aesthetics or publishability.
